candidato.titulo: New commentary calls for shift to nurse-sensitive outcome measures
candidato.resumo: Current health care metrics fail to capture the true value of acute and critical care nursing, evaluating the profession primarily by the absence of patient harm rather than positive clinical outcomes, according to a commentary in JAMA Internal Medicine.

texto_fonte:
New commentary calls for shift to nurse-sensitive outcome measures
Current health care metrics fail to capture the true value of acute and critical care nursing, evaluating the profession primarily by the absence of patient harm rather than positive clinical outcomes, according to a commentary in JAMA Internal Medicine.
Martha A.Q. Curley, Ph.D., RN, FAAN, professor in the Department of Family and Community Health and the Ruth M. Colket Endowed Chair in Pediatric Nursing at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, served as senior author of the commentary, which urges health systems, payers and credentialing bodies to adopt metrics that reflect the full scope of nursing practice—including surveillance, symptom management and care coordination.
Her co-authors include Lori Kennedy, Ph.D., RN, ACNP-BC, from the Center for Nursing Science at UC Davis Health and the Betty Irene Moore School of Nursing at UC Davis in Sacramento, California; and Laura Beth Kalvas, Ph.D., RN, from the Center for Nursing Excellence and the Center for Biobehavioral Health at the Abigail Wexner Research Institute at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio.
"At a time when health care professional burnout and turnover are high, our solution is to concentrate on what makes nursing the most trusted health care profession," the authors write. "Data drive accountability. We ask our physician colleagues to join in our call for change in how nursing quality is measured in hospital environments. The value of nursing care is not in the sum of harms prevented. It is in the sum of what nurses do."
The commentary highlights that traditional metrics—such as hospital-acquired infections or pressure injuries—force a defensive economic case for nursing investments, overlooking the critical role nurses play in early intervention and preventing clinical deterioration.
Drawing on nine core practice domains established by the American Academy of Nursing's Expert Panel on Acute and Critical Care, the authors call for a shift toward nurse-sensitive patient outcomes and invite physician colleagues to partner in reforming health care quality evaluation.
Publication details
Lori S. Kennedy et al., Time to Measure the Outcomes of What Nurses Really Do, JAMA Internal Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.5066
Journal information: JAMA Internal Medicine

Keeping jumping genes in place: New role for protein complex discovered
As much as half of the human genome is composed of so-called "jumping genes." These DNA sequences can make copies of themselves that are inserted back into the genome at another location, playing a significant functional role in creating the diversity that drives evolution and in regulating how other genes are turned on or off. However, their jumps can also make the genome less stable and create mutations that have been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, autoimmune disease and cancer.
So, what keeps these jumping genes—also known as transposable elements—from hopping around and breaking things like too many kids on a trampoline? New research, led by Penn State scientists and published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, has identified a new role for a complex of proteins as a suppressor of jumping gene activity.
"CCR4-NOT is a complex of proteins that has been well characterized in yeast," said Shardul Kulkarni, assistant research professor of biochemistry and molecular biology in the Penn State Eberly College of Science and the lead author of the paper. "In the past decade, its role in human cell lines has started to be explored, but those studies have focused mainly on characterizing its role in RNA processing and degradation. We wanted to learn more about its role in the nucleus of cells where it is involved in the production of RNA from a DNA template."
In yeast, CCR4-NOT's role has been characterized in multiple phases of gene regulation; it helps to control how RNA—the molecule that carries information from DNA out of the nucleus to perform cellular functions, including protein production—is produced in the nucleus of a cell, how that RNA gets transported out of the nucleus into the cell's cytoplasm, where it helps to translate the RNA into a protein and, eventually, degrade it, Kulkarni explained.
The cytoplasm is the viscous liquid that fills cells and contains the organelles that help carry out the cell's function; the nucleus is the organelle that contains the cell's genetic material.
Removing proteins unleashes gene activity
The team used a technique called auxin-induced degradation to individually knock down—or reduce expression of—CNOT1 and CNOT4, two components of the CCR4-NOT complex in a human cancer cell line obtained through the U.S. National Institutes of Health. The researchers genetically modified these two proteins to be versions that would be degraded within an hour when auxin was added to the cells. In previous work, they had shown that knockdown of these two components had opposite effects in the cell's cytoplasm, but they were surprised to see that knockdown of both proteins produced the same effect in the nucleus.
"We were surprised that knockdown of both CNOT1 and CNOT4 resulted in a rapid widespread increase of transcription across the genome," Kulkarni said, explaining that transcription is the process of producing RNA from a DNA template. "This included jumping genes, whose expression also increased. However, the expression of one set of genes was instead reduced. This family of genes—called the Kruppel-associated box-containing zinc nuclear finger (KZNF) family—is a known repressor of jumping gene activity."
Multiple defenses against jumping genes
The study demonstrated—for the first time—the role of the CCR4-NOT complex in suppressing jumping gene activity, likely through its regulation of the KZNF genes.
"The genome-wide increase in transcription, including jumping genes, is likely due to CCR4-NOT regulation of KZNF genes," Kulkarni said. "Our work reveals that a molecular complex best known for controlling RNA also acts as a guardian, helping prevent these genetic elements from being switched on. This newly identified role of CCR4-NOT is crucial for maintaining genome stability and preventing other potentially harmful effects of jumping genes.
"And there is a particularly interesting second layer: Our work suggests that CCR4-NOT doesn't just prevent these elements from being transcribed; it also helps control the stability of the RNA they produce. In other words, the complex provides multiple layers of defense against unwanted genetic activity."
Publication details
Shardul D. Kulkarni et al., CCR4-NOT is required for suppressing pervasive transcription and retrotransposable elements, Journal of Biological Chemistry (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jbc.2026.113289

texto_fonte:
The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed
Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.
Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.
From ATRIAS to Digit
My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.
We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.
With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?
Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.
Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.
ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics
Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.
Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.
Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins
As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.
After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.
In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.
Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.
I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.
Turning Digit Into a Product
I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.
Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility
We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.
While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok
I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.
Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.
Digit 5
Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.
Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok
Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.
Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.
Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.
Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.
The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics
Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.
All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.
The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.
When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics
Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.
With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.
What Comes After Digit 5
I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.
Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok
But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.
We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.
I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.
With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

texto_fonte:
Novo launcher Xodus Nexus permite rodar jogos do Xbox no Linux
Por Raphael Giannotti |
A comunidade open-source deu mais um passo importante para aproximar a biblioteca de jogos da Microsoft dos sistemas operacionais baseados em Linux. Isso acontece agora com o Xodus Nexus, um novo gerenciador de jogos de código aberto voltado especialmente para donos de consoles portáteis como o Steam Deck.
A ferramenta simplifica a instalação, o gerenciamento de assinaturas e a navegação da biblioteca do Xbox Game Pass diretamente pelo SteamOS e por distribuições Linux, eliminando a dependência de métodos complexos ou do uso exclusivo de navegadores web via nuvem.
App promete ser simples, mas intuitivo
Até então, acessar o ecossistema do Xbox no sistema operacional da Valve exigia configurações manuais trabalhosas para rodar o Xbox Cloud Gaming ou a instalação completa do Windows na máquina. O Xodus Nexus chega com uma interface gráfica intuitiva que integra as funcionalidades desenvolvidas pelo projeto Xodus, permitindo navegar pelo catálogo do serviço, autenticar a conta da Microsoft com segurança e gerenciar downloads com poucos cliques.
A interface foi projetada sob medida para telas sensíveis ao toque e navegação por controles, se adaptando perfeitamente ao modo de exibição de dispositivos portáteis.
Além da usabilidade melhorada, o gerenciador cuida automaticamente das camadas de tradução de software e da descriptografia dos arquivos nativos de jogos da loja da Microsoft. A plataforma faz o trabalho pesado de adaptar o sistema de chamadas da API do ecossistema Xbox para rodar em camadas como Wine e Proton, reduzindo a complexidade de instalação para o usuário final que busca executar jogos locais sem enfrentar incompatibilidades severas.
Essa novidade fortalece ainda mais a presença de alternativas ao ecossistema da Microsoft no cenário de jogos para PC. À medida que projetos comunitários evoluem, o SteamOS e o ecossistema Linux continuam ganhando espaço como uma plataforma sólida para jogar sem restrições.
Para quem acompanha os avanços nessa área, a recente ascensão dos consoles portáteis tem impulsionado desenvolvedores e empresas a investir no setor, com iniciativas que vão desde a expansão de compatibilidade em sistemas operacionais até projetos focados em levar jogos do Xbox e Game Pass ao Linux de forma cada vez mais acessível e nativa.

candidato.titulo: Mysterious AMD Zen 6 APU with 24GB of LPDDR5 memory appears in benchmarks — chip may be for next-gen Steam Deck or gaming handhelds
candidato.resumo: The engineering sample features six CPU cores, 24GB of LPDDR5 memory running at 9,600 MT/s, and an integrated GPU clocked at 2.4 GHz, although its connection to a future Steam Deck remains unconfirmed.

texto_fonte:
An AMD engineering sample has made an appearance in a listing on OpenBenchmarking. According to a report by TechPowerUp, the chip could potentially be a part of AMD’s upcoming Gainsborough family and a possible candidate for the next-generation Steam Deck handheld console. As per the OpenBenchmarking listing, the chip comes with a six-core, 12-thread processor paired with 24GB of high-speed LPDDR5 memory.
The engineering sample with part number 100-000001930-12_Y was tested on an AMD GBR-FF6-SKT validation board, with the CPU running at clock speeds of 2.4 GHz. The system also features four 6GB SK Hynix memory packages, resulting in 24GB of LPDDR5 memory running at 9,600 MT/s. That’s a big jump when compared to the current Steam Deck, which comes with 16GB of LPDDR5 memory running at 6,400 MT/s, alongside a four-core, eight-thread AMD Zen 2 processor.
The benchmark listing also provides some clues about the processor’s underlying architecture. As per Notebookcheck, the sample’s CPU microcode revision corresponds to AMD’s Family 1Ah, model DCh. Linux kernel changes indicate that this model falls within the range reserved for newer Zen 6 processors, suggesting that Gainsborough could use AMD’s next-generation CPU architecture. However, there is no clarity or any confirmation whether it will use standard Zen 6 cores or the denser Zen 6C variant.
The integrated GPU is listed with a clock speed of 2,400 MHz, although its architecture and compute unit count remain unknown. The sample was tested using the GpuTest benchmark suite on Ubuntu 24.04 at 1024 x 768 resolution, resulting in scores of 3,871 in GiMark, 3,508 in FurMark, and 9,319 in TessMark. While the FurMark score is comparable to the original Stam Deck, we can’t really come to any conclusions at this point, as the tests were conducted on an engineering platform using development software rather than a finished handheld. For now, the results do not establish how the chip would perform in games, as power limits, cooling, driver maturity, and the final GPU configuration all contribute to the performance in a compact gaming device.
If these specifications carry over to a future Steam Deck, the additional CPU cores along with the larger and faster memory would provide a meaningful hardware upgrade. That being said, neither AMD nor Valve have confirmed a connection between the Gainsborough family and a future Steam Deck. Thus, it is best to take this with a grain of salt and wait until there is more concrete information in the future.

candidato.titulo: NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos
candidato.resumo: NASA's stunning new gallery of 16 galaxies reveals colossal black hole jets, explosive star formation, and spectacular cosmic collisions through the combined power of Chandra, James Webb, Hubble, and other telescopes. These extraordinary images expose the hidden forces shaping galaxies across the universe and offer clues about the Milky Way's own past and future.

texto_fonte:
NASA reveals 16 stunning galaxies hiding cosmic chaos
- Date:
- October 20, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA's stunning new gallery of 16 galaxies reveals colossal black hole jets, explosive star formation, and spectacular cosmic collisions through the combined power of Chandra, James Webb, Hubble, and other telescopes. These extraordinary images expose the hidden forces shaping galaxies across the universe and offer clues about the Milky Way's own past and future.
- Share:
Some galaxies glow with sweeping spiral arms, while others are shaped by violent collisions, powerful black holes, and explosive bursts of star formation. A newly released collection of 16 images from NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes reveals the extraordinary diversity of these cosmic structures.
Like precious gemstones, galaxies come in many shapes and sizes, each with characteristics that tell a story about its history. Astronomers generally classify them into three major groups. Spiral galaxies, including our Milky Way, have winding arms extending from their centers. Elliptical galaxies typically contain older stars and are often thought to form through galactic mergers. Irregular galaxies have less orderly structures and can display a wide variety of cosmic activity.
Much as gemstones preserve clues about the geological processes that shaped Earth over billions of years, galaxies hold evidence of the forces that have shaped the universe. Studying these distant systems helps astronomers piece together the Milky Way's history and better understand what may await our galaxy in the distant future.
NASA Combines Chandra, Webb, and Hubble to Reveal Galactic Secrets
The new gallery features 16 images that bring together observations from some of the world's most powerful telescopes. Each includes X-ray measurements gathered by Chandra during its decades of operation in space.
These observations are combined with data from NASA's James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes, IXPE (Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array), and additional observatories operating on Earth and in space.
X-ray observations are especially valuable because they reveal extreme activity that other types of light can miss. Chandra can detect enormous clouds of gas heated to millions of degrees by powerful winds from massive stars, material expelled by supermassive black holes, and debris from stellar explosions. These processes also help spread chemical elements through space, including elements that ultimately become part of planets, the air we breathe, and our own bodies.
By combining X-rays with observations at other wavelengths, astronomers can see more of what is happening inside galaxies. The resulting images reveal how these vast systems form stars, interact with their surroundings, and change over billions of years.
Spiral Galaxies Reveal Explosive Star Formation
Several images highlight the remarkable activity taking place inside spiral galaxies. Messier 33 and NGC 3938 are viewed almost directly from above, allowing astronomers to examine their sweeping arms and identify regions containing energetic pairs of stars and the aftermath of stellar explosions.
Other galaxies reveal how their internal structures can help drive the birth of new stars. NGC 1672 and NGC 1385 are barred spiral galaxies, meaning they contain elongated central structures made of stars, gas, and dust. These bars can channel material toward the inner regions, providing fuel for intense episodes of star formation.
NGC 4725 demonstrates another way galaxies can produce new stars. Its observations reveal how an earlier encounter with another galaxy can disturb gas and stimulate star formation.
The collection also includes dramatic side views of NGC 4631 (the Whale Galaxy) and Messier 82 (the Cigar Galaxy). These galaxies feature enormous halos and powerful winds of gas heated to millions of degrees. Driven by intense stellar explosions, these outflows can carry material thousands of light-years into space, spreading important chemical elements into the regions between galaxies.
Supermassive Black Holes Blast Energy Across Galaxies
Some of the most dramatic features in the gallery come from the enormous black holes lurking at the centers of galaxies.
When these black holes actively consume surrounding material, their central regions become extremely energetic. Known as active galactic nuclei, these bright and powerful galactic cores can launch jets of particles and enormous outbursts that influence conditions across their host galaxies.
Centaurus A provides a striking example. Observations from Chandra and IXPE reveal a powerful stream of high-energy particles shooting tens of thousands of light-years into space from the galaxy's central region.
In Messier 106, jets launched from the central supermassive black hole interact with and heat surrounding gas. This activity produces unusual spiral structures that differ from the familiar arms normally associated with spiral galaxies.
The famous Sombrero Galaxy (Messier 104) offers another remarkable view. A supermassive black hole sits within its immense central concentration of stars, while Chandra's X-ray observations reveal a widespread halo of gas heated to millions of degrees and the hot remains of stars. These features surround the galaxy's prominent bands of dust, providing a deeper look at the energetic environment hidden within its elegant appearance.
Violent Galaxy Collisions Offer a Glimpse of the Milky Way's Future
Not every galaxy evolves peacefully. Some undergo enormous transformations as gravity pulls neighboring galaxies together, distorts their structures, or strips away the gas needed to create new stars.
Arp 143 captures the aftermath of a particularly dramatic encounter. A direct galactic collision produced an expanding ring, similar to ripples spreading outward after an impact. The disturbance also triggered waves of new star formation.
Other images show the chaotic consequences of galaxies merging. NGC 3256 and II Zw 096, the latter containing a powerful burst of star formation hidden behind thick dust, provide examples of the violent interactions that were especially common in the early universe.
These collisions also offer clues about the Milky Way's possible future. Our galaxy is expected to merge with the neighboring Andromeda galaxy billions of years from now, and observing other galactic mergers helps scientists understand how such an encounter could unfold.
The gallery includes several other unusual systems. NGC 1569 serves as a nearby example for investigating the intense episodes of star formation that occurred in young galaxies billions of years ago. NGC 660 displays a rare "polar ring" structure, with a ring of stars orbiting around the galaxy's poles rather than following its main plane.
Messier 90 illustrates a different kind of galactic transformation. As it travels through the Virgo Cluster, the galaxy is losing the gas it needs to form new stars. Its movement through the cluster strips away this material, potentially changing how the galaxy evolves.
Together, these 16 cosmic portraits show that galaxies are far from static collections of stars. They are constantly influenced by gravity, stellar explosions, black holes, and interactions with neighboring systems. By revealing these processes in remarkable detail, NASA's Chandra and its partner telescopes are helping astronomers understand the forces that shape galaxies, including our own.

candidato.titulo: A quantum computing feat brings the ‘megaquops’ era a step closer
candidato.resumo: Error correction creates qubits that glitch only 5 out of a million times, the first step toward a new phase for quantum computing.

texto_fonte:
Quantum computers capable of doing a million reliable operations could bring about a new stage of quantum calculation. That “megaquop” regime — as it’s called — isn’t here yet. But scientists just took a significant step toward it.
A quantum computer built by the company Quantinuum has error rates so low that it could perform a million operations with only about five errors, researchers report in a paper posted October 19 on the company’s website and arXiv.org.
“These statistics are consistent with this being a good building block for that megaquop machine,” says quantum physicist David Hayes of Quantinuum, who is based in Broomfield, Colo. In order to reach that regime, however, such computers will need to be scaled up.
Quantinuum’s computer, known as Helios, is made of electrically charged atoms, called ions, hovering over a chip. Those ions serve as the 98 quantum bits, or qubits, of the computer. But, like all qubits, those ions are finicky. Their states are delicate and can flip unintentionally and mess up calculations, like a 0 randomly switching to a 1.
A technique called quantum error correction tackles this by combining multiple error-prone qubits into one, forming a supercharged unit called a logical qubit that is less prone to mistakes. (For those who grew up on 1990s TV, it’s a bit like how Captain Planet is born from the combined powers of the gang of Planeteers.)
Logical qubits come in different sizes, integrating a given number of physical qubits — the ions, in this case. Each time a logical qubit is scaled up, going, say, from seven physical qubits to 19, the error rate drops by a factor called lambda. A previous demonstration of error correction by Google, reported in Nature in 2024, had a lambda of about 2, meaning errors were cut in half each time the logical qubits were scaled up.
Quantinuum’s computer has a lambda of about 10. So errors dropped quickly when the researchers made larger logical qubits. A logical qubit composed of 37 physical qubits had just 5 errors in a million operations — close to what would be needed for the megaquop regime. However, that experiment involved only a single logical qubit. Reaching the megaquop regime could possibly involve around 50 to 100 logical qubits.
The large value of lambda means that achieving a desired error rate takes fewer physical qubits, says Ken Brown, a quantum engineer at Duke University and a scientific adviser for the company Logiqal who was not involved with the research. “That’s a huge savings in the overall number of qubits you would need. So that’s what’s exciting.”

texto_fonte:
Does “free tokens” mean anything to you? If so, read on. What about quality Windows on Arm gaming? Get in line. Solid productivity? You’re in the right place. The Surface Laptop Ultra and its RTX Spark brethren are here.
I tested Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra for about a week, pushing it to its limits. You can read my full review here, but be warned: it clocks in at about 5,000 words, only because I’m an obsessive productivity nerd. If I want to know what makes it tick, why shouldn’t you?
My editors suggested something a bit more succinct, summing up the high points of the review. So here’s the story of the Surface Laptop Ultra and its brethren: a surprisingly average CPU, paired with a terrific GPU and good battery life, but with all the qualms Windows on Arm brings.
I thought, oh, Arm — haven’t all the problems been solved with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips? Apparently not! I was forced to work with a beta version of Adobe Premiere, so there’s development work to be done.
Here’s what you need to know about the Surface Laptop Ultra.
1.) The base price is $2,599. It tops out at $5,899.99
Mark Hachman / Foundry
It’s the K-shaped economy in a nutshell. My family produced gasps when I told them the price was $2,599 price. When I explained that was the cheapest model, they gasped again. But for the puffy vest crowd swarming San Francisco for TechCrunch Disrupt, $6,000 or so is just the cost of doing business, especially if they can do other productive activities as AI agents code, chat, and communicate.
Still, one of the gaming laptops I tested against — the ROG Strix SCAR 16, with a Core Ultra 9 275HX, RTX 5090, and 2TB of storage — costs “just” $4,499.99. But Microsoft will give you $1,000 for your MacBook Pro as a trade-in!
2.) Its chip is already a year old… kind of
Project Digits, which Nvidia launched in January 2025, shipped as the DGX Spark workstation a year ago. DGX Spark, like the RTX Spark, combined a CPU (co-designed with Mediatek) with with an RTX “Blackwell” GPU (designed wholly by Nvidia). The workstation ran Linux. This runs Windows.
Nvidia
Tried and true? Outdated? You make the call. But it does keep up with the big boys, generally.
3.) Single-core CPU performance is half that of the Mac
Modern games take advantage of everything inside the PC. But the operating system needs to run on relatively ancient PCs, and most of Windows seems to be clustered together in just a few instruction threads. Put another way, some of your day-to-day PC experience depends on how fast each individual processor core runs.
In the first day or so with the Surface Laptop Ultra, it felt a bit laggy. I wondered why. Even now the Start menu opens and closes responsively, but switching between menu items in the Settings menu is noticeably slow. Single-core CPU performance matters and the N1X chip powering the Surface Laptop Ultra stinks. That’s indicated in the chart below, which is hierarchically sorted by multicore performance, not single-core.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
Macs feel faster because of the tight integration between Apple’s operating system and chips. Apple Silicon is also far beyond the Windows world. The N1X’s score (96) is way behind Apple’s M6 score (220), according to CPU Monkey.
New MacBook Pros are rumored to be launched later this month, too. In terms of responsiveness, the Surface Laptop Ultra will never keep up.
4.) Graphics performance is very impressive
There are many ways to measure laptop graphics, but I like ComfyUI as a metric. It’s an application for generating text-to-video output — AI slop. However, the app includes a built-in benchmark that averages the time for a number of representative runs, including a warmup.
I took several gaming laptops (specs listed below) and ran that benchmark on them. Acer’s laptop is the most recent with a creator-class RTX 5060 inside it, but the Laptop Ultra is in another tier, closer to the massive Asus ROG Strix at the top of the heap.
ComfyUI’s latest version does explicitly support RTX Spark architecture, so there’s that. But optimizations like this benefit the user regardless. You can see my review for other comparisons.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
5.) App incompatibility may still be a thing
When Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chip first debuted (even before the X1 Elite), some applications written for X86 chips from AMD and Intel wouldn’t run on Arm. Some of that was alleviated by Microsoft’s Prism emulator in Windows, which translated X86 instructions to Arm native code. But just like a conversation with someone who doesn’t speak the same language as you, translation slowed the process down.
I was surprised to find that the RTX Spark family of laptops may have the same experience, though this time from a GPU perspective. Adobe Premiere needed a special beta to run. Without it, Premiere complained of an unsupported GPU. ComfyUI specifically supported the RTX Spark. I don’t think that games will have any issues with the RTX Spark, but I’m not entirely certain we’ve put this issue to bed, either.
6.) It’s a perfectly functional productivity laptop
The Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t just for AI nerds. The laptop functioned perfectly well as an ordinary, day-to-day 15-inch laptop. It is more than four pounds, however. While it’s compact, it’s neither thin nor especially light. I think of it as a relative to the Surface Laptop Studio, but without the cool pull-forward screen.
Battery life was about 10 hours while performing a set benchmark simulating office work, so that’s fine.
7.) Memory matters with AI more than you’d think
Why wait all this time to discuss AI? Because I’m still convinced that the lower-end models of the Surface Laptop Ultra and its competition should be seen more as “ordinary” laptops, while the pricey, high-end models lend themselves more to AI.
The RTX Spark architecture uses shared memory, so the laptop I was given with 32GB of RAM splits that between the CPU and GPU. A gaming laptop with a dedicated GPU contains its own VRAM. That’s a subtle but significant difference!
Matt Smith / Foundry
Microsoft believes that you’ll be able to run AI (agents or LLMs) at the same time as you work elsewhere on the machine such a web browser. I did load the Hermes agent and let it do its thing while I worked elsewhere, but I don’t really know if AI performance suffered as a result. I didn’t have enough time to test this as thoroughly as I would like.
The fact is, though, that the largest AI models can demand more storage and RAM than compressed, quantized AI models. And if there’s a super-cool AI model that everyone’s talking about, you might not be able to run it if you opt for a low-end machine.
8.) The cultural aspect troubles me
The compelling reason to use local AI is you can generate “free tokens” without a cloud subscription. You don’t need to be connected to the internet. But there is a price to be paid, both in power consumption and fan noise.
Pexels
I still wonder what that looks like in the real world. I caught the Surface Laptop Ultra pulling about 130 watts while gaming, and I suspect that intensive LLM work will require the same.
Imagine traveling to Asia, seated next to someone using a Laptop Ultra. Limited connectivity, so they’ve gone to local AI. Is there enough power from the seatback to even allow this? Will the laptop fans howl while you’re trying to sleep? What will your neighborhood coffee shop be like with tech bros all maxing out their laptop cooling? It’s like a little portable data center, but right next your ear.
The big brains who think through these things never seem to understand that consumers like technology when it works for them. I just hope that ends up being the case.

candidato.titulo: Why teaching AI about symmetry could make prenatal diagnosis more reliable
candidato.resumo: A model developed by researchers at MIT and Boston Children's Hospital adjusts scans on the fly to track fetal movement, potentially sparing families repeat hospital visits.

texto_fonte:
Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain.
In a routine prenatal ultrasound, the sonographer will flag possible brain abnormalities for additional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). But imperfect imaging can result in missed or incorrect diagnoses.
To assist with the early detection and treatment of these abnormalities, researchers at MIT, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Inria have developed and trained a deep learning model called E(3)-Pose that helps image the fetus’s head while it’s in motion to capture a high-resolution image that the radiologist can examine. A paper about the work was presented at the 2026 European Conference on Computer Vision.
“One of the problems with having the baby move is that the slices are all over the place,” says first author Ramya Muthukrishnan. Muthukrishnan is an MIT PhD student in the lab of Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Polina Golland, who is a principal investigator at the MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).
By slices, Muthukrishnan is referring to a series of 2D images taken during a fetal MRI scan. These 2D planes stacked together effectively make up one high-resolution, 3D image of the fetus’s head. But if the head shifts during imaging, each 2D image “slice” could end up being taken from a different angle, resulting in gaps in the final scan and unusual slice orientation. These problems may cause the physician reviewing the MRI to miss or incorrectly diagnose a pathology in the fetal brain.
“There are very fine details that you need a very good volumetric picture of the brain to see,” explains Muthukrishnan. “If you have coverage gaps, you can’t see critical regions, and you need to be able to see well to detect abnormal development.”
What makes E(3)-Pose particularly good at tracking fetal motion is its focus on physics. Rather than simply training the model to learn physics from the data, the very principles of physics are baked into the neural network: left-right symmetry of the fetal head is embedded in the model architecture, making it easier for the model to accurately identify the brain’s orientation.
When Muthukrishnan began working on the project at the start of her PhD, she had no background in physics, let alone MRI physics. Most of her experience was in computer science. “I was surprised when I had to go and implement this on the scanner,” she recalls. “I was not prepared for how many times I would crash the scanner because putting things on hardware and getting it to work on hardware is a different beast than training a model to run on data on a GPU.”
Despite the challenges, Muthukrishnan persisted. She remembers shadowing a radiologist who performed fetal MRI scans at Boston Children’s Hospital at the start of her PhD and observing the shared frustration of the patient and radiologist: the pregnant mother felt uncomfortable after spending an hour in an MRI, only to quit the scan halfway; the radiologist was unable to procure a full, high-quality MRI to monitor the development of the fetus.
“Seeing frustration about it helped me decide what I wanted to do with my PhD, because it felt like this was a pain point,” Muthukrishnan says.
Fortunately, she had help: Co-author Borjan Gagoski, an assistant professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at Boston Children's Hospital, developed a sequence that acquires additional MRI scans to assist with training E(3)-Pose and worked with Muthukrishnan to help troubleshoot the scanner whenever it crashed. Co-author and Boston Children’s Research Assistant Aryn Lee recruited the pregnant volunteers and assisted with acquiring each of the MRI scans. Senior authors who helped guide the project include Elfar Adalsteinsson, MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science; Ellen Grant, the Käthe Beutler Professor of Pediatrics and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School; and Golland. Benjamin Billot, a researcher at Inria and a former postdoc in Golland’s group, helped Muthukrishnan get started with the initial method he developed.
“Ramya’s work elegantly combines geometric concepts like equivariance and symmetry with the power of deep learning to change how MRI scanners acquire the images, and to ultimately help the physicians detect and treat problems early in development. It’s an impressive research project that is deep and fundamental in how it models image acquisition, with clear clinical impact,” says Golland.
Grant, who directs the Fetal Neonatal Neuroimaging and Developmental Science Center (FNNDSC) at Boston Children’s, adds that Muthukrishnan’s work “will automate fetal brain MRI, replacing today's slow, manual process with faster and more comfortable scans for mothers, while also providing higher-quality images for radiologists to interpret.”
E(3)-Pose’s applications could extend beyond motion tracking for fetal MRIs. It could assist with imaging other hard-to-image anatomy, and even autonomous driving applications, where limited sensors need to capture noisy, 3D data in order to track 3D objects.
For now, Muthukrishnan hopes to improve E(3)-Pose so that it can help with imaging second-trimester or younger fetuses, as the model is primarily trained on third trimester fetuses. Second-trimester fetuses are “so small, they move around a lot more because there’s more space in the uterus,” Muthukrishnan says. “They’re more important to focus on because the earlier you detect brain abnormalities, the easier it is to intervene.”
This work is supported by the MIT Jameel Clinic, the MIT Takeda Program, the Chou Family Transformative Research Fund, the National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering, and the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

candidato.titulo: Middle East fuel crunch drives solar push in tiny Fiji
candidato.resumo: Power cables weave through palm trees high above Fiji's Rukurukulevu village, linking residents to the national grid and a select few to solar panels.

texto_fonte:
Middle East fuel crunch drives solar push in tiny Fiji
Power cables weave through palm trees high above Fiji's Rukurukulevu village, linking residents to the national grid and a select few to solar panels.
The settlement of about 400 people finally electrified its last building this year—a kindergarten, just meters from the sea.
But residents are struggling to keep the lights on as the Middle East war and other factors push up energy bills.
It is challenging Fiji's reliance on imported fossil fuels and driving a push toward renewables in the resource-scarce island nation.
"The prices of electricity here in Fiji (are) very high," village spokesman Vereniki Nalio told AFP.
"Some houses, they got FJ$100 (US$44) and over. The church, community halls and church minister's house, they've got about FJ$200, nearly FJ$300, for a month."
Nalio said he paid about FJ$60 per month for electricity—"very, very high."
Opposite his home stands another small house with one big difference: past the clothes hanging on the clothesline lies a small array of solar panels.
Another home across the road boasts an even larger installation, showing how some in the village are seeking to move away from dependence on the grid.
Since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, fuel shipments from the Gulf have slowed.
Nalio said the subsequent global energy squeeze had led villagers to consider switching to renewables.
A basic solar power system costs around FJ$3,000, a higher upfront cost but an increasingly reasonable price to pay for theoretically unlimited, free electricity.
"They said we had no more fuel, no more gasoline would come to Fiji. So at that time we think about solar," Nalio said.
He added that the village hoped to install solar panels on communal buildings to reduce the shared cost of powering them.
Pointing to the sky, Nalio said Rukurukulevu should not have to import its energy.
"Solar is already here."
Rush for renewables
Fiji hosted this month's "pre-COP" United Nations climate summit, where Pacific Island nations pressed for faster access to climate financing for projects such as renewable energy.
The event was a precursor to next month's main COP event in Turkey, where organizers will push for member states to commit to electrification—replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives.
Symbolizing the challenges the Pacific faces, a major power outage on the second day of the event plunged the 4,000 attendees into darkness.
Government minister Ro Filipe Tuisawau blamed Fiji's rising energy prices on overreliance on fossil fuels and El Niño.
The cyclical climate phenomenon is particularly strong this year and has brought weather patterns that are drying up Fiji's hydroelectric dams.
They "will face a critical situation" if rainfall does not increase by mid-November, Tuisawau, whose remit covers public works, weather services and transport, told AFP.
"We would probably go into water rationing and power rationing in the next, maybe, four weeks if the situation doesn't change," he said.
"The hotels can enjoy (it) now, but we will cut off their water to the pool."
Fiji spends as much as 12% of its GDP on importing fossil fuels—"a huge drain on our resources," Tuisawau said.
The country is aiming for 90% renewable energy generation by 2035 and plans to spend FJ$2 billion on solar and hydropower development in the next decade.
That includes investing at least FJ$460 million in solar farms in the next four years, as well as FJ$650 million on two new dams and more than FJ$700 million to expand its main transmission lines.
For now, though, many islanders are still facing the sharp end of Fiji's energy crisis, Tuisawau acknowledged.
"With the price, with geopolitical issues, and in addition El Niño right now, it's a very difficult situation," he said.

candidato.titulo: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
candidato.resumo: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

texto_fonte:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
